talks.title: PANEL DISCUSSION | Cybersecurity in UNECE R155 Agricultural relevant Vehicles
talks.teaser: Industry panelists discuss offline updates, certificate trust and threat motives for farm vehicles under UNECE R155.
talks.summary:
The panel, moderated by John Potter, brought together engineers and standards leads from agricultural equipment makers and industry associations to discuss cybersecurity under UNECE R155. The opening presenter gave background on the AEF, an industry body that standardizes tractor and implement electronics so equipment from different brands works together. He described conformance testing labs and a shared public key infrastructure that issues certificates authorizing implement functions such as steering or ground speed control. Runtime security and encryption are not yet in place, and work on runtime signatures and gigabit Ethernet is ongoing.

Operational limits came next. Machines often stay offline for long stretches and are used in short seasonal windows, which makes timely updates hard, and a single failed patch could make farmers reluctant to accept future ones. Brad Nielsen contrasted top-down risk assessments with bottom-up hardware security designs, since some machines remain in service for decades. Ransomware was described as the most common motive, and nation-state interest in farm data was raised as a concern. The panel also referred to reports of stolen tractors in Ukraine being remotely disabled, without confirming them. Certificate revocation is largely unimplemented because offline machines lack a trusted time source.

Late questions covered shorter TLS certificate lifetimes, which panelists said mainly affect cloud connections, and whether conformance testing requires penetration tests; it does not. The takeaway was that multi-brand interoperability depends on shared standards, testing and a clear certificate lifecycle, and that automotive could learn from this approach to federated identity.

talks.title: Simulating and Evaluating Incident Response for Automotive Systems
talks.teaser: Compares tabletop, incident simulation, and red-team playbooks for training and evaluating automotive security incident intake.
talks.summary:
Rising connected-vehicle incidents and large-scale breaches motivate treating automotive product security incidents as a when-not-if problem. The speakers contrast Carriad’s praised handling of a researcher-reported Volkswagen data exposure—aided by security.txt and fast technical response—with industry data showing more remote attacks and fleet-scale impact.

They present three exercise types: low-effort tabletop discussions, mid-tier incident simulations with partial awareness and injectable stressors, and high-effort red teaming with limited observability. Red, blue, and white teams follow playbooks that start with external stimuli, observe process performance, and optionally degrade availability to test resilience.

Walkthroughs target the automotive incident intake path, from a red-team remote code execution report with proof of concept through triage, stakeholder notification, and timing metrics, to an angry customer privacy complaint when key managers are absent. Evaluation covers contact discoverability, response speed, reporter communication, stakeholder coverage, and gaps between documented and executed process. They recommend tabletop exercises to learn procedures and recurring incident simulations for realistic practice, noting tier suppliers often lag OEMs and that hands-on exercise beats passive training.

talks.title: Under the Hood Tracking API Exploits Before They Hit the Road
talks.teaser: Examines how weak vehicle APIs enable remote commands and VIN-based abuse, and how to detect it using telematics context.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how application programming interfaces in the connected-vehicle ecosystem open doors for attackers. These interfaces power remote commands, software updates, EV charging and dealer tools. Their scale and simple identifiers, such as a VIN or license plate, make them attractive. Two real cases were walked through: a lookup endpoint that returned owner details with no authorization or rate limits, and a plate-based pivot that reached remote vehicle functions.

A standard API gateway checks identity and request rates but ignores the vehicle's state. Implausible activity was shown as a warning sign, such as a remote unlock issued while a car was driving, a charging command sent when the car reported it was unplugged, or a remote start hundreds of kilometers from the last known location. The proposed defence has six parts: a live inventory of APIs and vehicles, correlation of API calls with telematics, attention to common API flaws, detection tuning from production and purple-team work, shared standards, and selective AI for triage.

In the question session, the speakers said APIs bring convenience and innovation but widen the attack surface. Automotive API flaws can have physical safety consequences, and chargers, dealers and energy participants add exposure, so responsibility is shared across the ecosystem.

talks.title: Source vs Binary code analysis Challenges and Solutions within the Software Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Compares source and binary code analysis for automotive supply chains and shows how SBOMs and VEX support vulnerability management.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at vulnerability management in automotive software supply chains, where an ECU can combine in-house code, open-source components, third-party libraries and proprietary software. The speaker, a product manager for automotive vulnerability management, notes that many buyers receive ECU firmware only as binaries, so they cannot see what is inside without a software bill of materials. She recommends standard formats such as CycloneDX and SPDX, and generating these lists automatically wherever possible.

The core of the talk compares the two analysis approaches. Source code analysis suits open-source components and catches developer mistakes during development, but it misses compiled and runtime issues. Binary analysis works where source is unavailable and can reveal hidden components, though it lacks data-flow context and deployability information. Two examples show the gap: in the Log4Shell case, source scanning misses runtime-loaded dependencies, while in the Heartbleed case, binary scanning finds the vulnerable library but not the source-level pattern. Combining both is presented as defense in depth.

The final part covers what happens after a scan returns a long vulnerability list. The speaker explains that teams must judge exploitability, and that VEX statements let them ask suppliers whether a component is actually affected or why a risk was accepted. Machine-readable advisories can then feed the same workflow. In the Q&A, she said binary tools handle open-source components well but are less reliable for proprietary automotive files. Her takeaways: standardize SBOMs, use both analysis methods, and adopt standards and APIs early.

talks.title: Automotive Ethernet Security Revisited New Protocols, New Attacks, and Advanced Scapy Techniques
talks.teaser: Shows how the Scapy toolchain tests automotive Ethernet ECUs, covering DoIP, SOME/IP, UDS and certificate handling.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Neils and Yonas, looks at penetration testing automotive Ethernet with the open-source Scapy library and its automotive extensions. It starts with how Scapy grew from IP support into CAN, ISO-TP, UDS and diagnostics over IP, SOME/IP and SecOC. The speakers explain why automotive Ethernet changes the attack surface: point-to-point links, much higher data rates, and many stacked protocol layers that each add parsing and handshake complexity.

The middle of the talk compares overhead. A two-byte UDS request fits in a CAN frame of roughly 14 bytes, but over plain DoIP the overhead reaches 672 bytes, and over TLS it rises to 6,700 bytes. Scapy's DoIP socket handles routing activation and TCP handshakes automatically, with optional TLS. Automatons can act as a fake HTTP server for over-the-air update clients, or as a SOME/IP rest bus simulator so that ECUs will start. The speakers also show malformed-certificate testing for UDS authentication, randomness checks with the NIST statistical test suite, and note that SecOC implementations differ between OEMs, so no out-of-the-box version exists.

The closing points are practical. TLS without mutual authentication adds little, so responsibilities between TLS and UDS must be defined clearly. An HSM that handles certificates can become a single point of failure, and ECUs must be able to recover from denial-of-service attacks rather than staying in a degraded mode. The Q&A touched on post-quantum cryptography, which Scapy would inherit from its underlying crypto libraries, and on regulatory handling of attack detection.

talks.title: The Cyber Resilience Act and its Implications on the Automotive Industry
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The Cyber Resilience Act and its Implications on the Automotive Industry.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Stefan Ross, a Senior Manager at Deloitte specializing in secure product engineering and regulatory frameworks, examines the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and its direct and indirect ramifications for the automotive industry. Hosted by Santosh Mador, the session details how shifting business models—such as OEMs evolving into broader mobility service providers and supplying components outside standard vehicle architectures—place automotive companies within the CRA's scope. The speaker analyzes interactions between the CRA, UNECE UN R155, and ISO/SAE 21434, offering guidance on building unified product security architectures rather than isolated compliance silos.

### Key Topics
- **Automotive Regulatory Landscape**: Traditional type approvals under UN R155 and ISO/SAE 21434 govern vehicle categories M, N, and L. However, emerging regional standards (such as China's GB 44495 and India's AIS 189) alongside sector standards like ISO 24882 for agricultural vehicles introduce compounding regulatory complexity.
- **Scope and Exclusions of the CRA**: Entered into force in November 2024 as an EU regulation directly applicable across member states, the CRA covers connected hardware and software products with digital elements. While vehicles covered under EU Regulation 2019/2144 are exempted under the *lex specialis* principle, out-of-scope categories (e.g., special-purpose vehicles, agricultural vehicles, off-the-shelf components, external digital services, and B2B components) fall squarely under the CRA.
- **Core Requirements & Penalties**: The CRA mandates security by design, at least five years of product security support/updates, Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), vulnerability management, and absence of known exploitable vulnerabilities. Non-compliance risks fines up to €15 million or 2.5% of global annual turnover, alongside the potential loss of CE marking required for EU market access.
- **Mapping to ISO/SAE 21434**: While many CRA security principles map conceptually to ISO/SAE 21434, the CRA differs significantly by imposing concrete timelines, legal obligations across economic operators (manufacturers, distributors, importers), customer communication baselines, market surveillance conformity assessments, and direct reporting obligations.
- **Strategic Architecture (MVC Pattern)**: Rather than maintaining fragmented compliance teams for each standard (UN R155, GB, CRA), organizations should adopt a decoupled framework akin to Model-View-Controller (MVC): a strong core Product Security Target Operating Model (Model), tailored via controllers to meet specific regional or product regulatory views.

### Technical Details & Implementation Deadlines
- **Deadlines**: The final deadline for all CRA obligations is December 2027, but incident and vulnerability reporting requirements take effect earlier (September 2027). During the Q&A, it was highlighted that early notification to CSIRTs/ENISA within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited incident is mandated.
- **Harmonized Standards**: Harmonized horizontal standards (covering risk assessment, vulnerability handling, and supplier management) and vertical product standards are being drafted but may only be released shortly before enforcement.
- **Conformity Assessments**: Approximately 90% of products falling under the default category will require self-assessment for CE marking compliance, whereas critical categories will face third-party conformity assessments.
- **B2B and Economic Roles**: The CRA applies across B2B and B2C settings. Suppliers delivering connected sub-products or placing components on the EU market operate as manufacturers under EU product law guidelines (such as the Blue Guide).

### Takeaways
Automotive manufacturers and suppliers cannot rely solely on vehicle type-approval exemptions. If an organization manufactures or imports connected software, hardware, or mobility services used outside vehicle-type approval scopes, CRA compliance is mandatory. Organizations should leverage existing ISO/SAE 21434 maturity as a foundational baseline, extend shift-left security directly into business and architectural decisions, and build unified, reusable security capabilities to address emerging global regulations without creating redundant compliance overhead.

talks.title: Exploit Story | AutoRFKiller The Tool That Unlocked Thousands of Cars and Earned Me Two CVEs
talks.teaser: A researcher traces aftermarket learning-code car alarms from personal discovery through open-source tooling and coordinated disclosure.
talks.summary:
The presentation follows discovery that a Kia Soluto aftermarket key fob used learning codes rather than rolling codes on sub-gigahertz RF, centered on chips such as the HS2240 at 370 MHz. Early replay proof at a dealership stalled when local Kia staff and suppliers showed little grasp of automotive CVE processes, pushing the researcher toward public release and tool building.

Work progressed from custom GNU Radio blocks and a Python CLI to Auto RF Killer, combining learning-code brute force—tuned via reverse-engineered ASK framing and encoding—with handling for fixed and rolling-code weaknesses. A live demo targets EB527-class fobs with HackRF, shrinking attack runtime through millisecond delays. The speaker maps Ecuador’s tier-one and tier-two supply chain to Chinese aftermarket remotes, notes widespread theft linked to replay familiarity, and describes collision risk across roughly one million 20-bit learning-code combinations.

Practitioners hear a disclosure arc through ASRG, two published automotive CVEs, press attention, and later paid review of a replacement rolling-code design that never shipped. Takeaways stress verifying aftermarket alarms, understanding learning versus rolling code, and when full disclosure becomes necessary if OEM and dealer channels stay silent.

talks.title: SBOMs in the Automotive Industry Real World Insights and Recommendations
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in SBOMs in the Automotive Industry Real World Insights and Recommendations.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session, Cortez Fraser Jr., Director of Product at FOSSA and former cybersecurity architect at GE Power, presents practical recommendations and insights into the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) lifecycle within the automotive industry. Driven by major supply chain incidents such as the SolarWinds compromise and Log4j, as well as regulations like Executive Order 14028, CISA minimum elements, the European Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and UN R155, automotive OEMs and suppliers must evolve beyond reactive manual manifest reviews. The talk lays out a three-stage maturity progression: SBOM generation and distribution, internal SBOM aggregation and vulnerability triage, and external supplier SBOM ingestion and policy enforcement.

### Key Topics
- **Regulatory & Security Drivers:** Shifts spurred by Executive Order 14028, CISA requirements, and UN R155 mandate visibility into critical components and supply chains.
- **Standards and Formats:** Primary standards include SPDX (noted for strong licensing support) and CycloneDX (noted for vulnerability reporting and backward compatibility).
- **Static vs. Dynamic Metadata:** Differentiating static components (package name, version, license) from dynamic attributes (vulnerability status, support status, end-of-life notices).
- **VEX and VDR:** Combining Vulnerability Disclosure Reports (VDR)—which supply CVE details, CVSS scores, and affected versions—with Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) statements asserting status (e.g., affected, not affected, under investigation, fixed) and justifications (e.g., inline mitigations).
- **Unique Component Identification:** Relying on Package URLs (PURL) or OmniBOR IDs over plain package names or CPEs, while addressing limitations with generic PURLs and commercial packages.

### Technical Details
- **Stage 1: Generation & Distribution:** SBOM generation is recommended immediately after the build phase and prior to deployment to ensure production accuracy. For automotive embedded systems, non-package-managed ecosystems (such as Yocto, Buildroot, and custom Linux distributions) pose major identification hurdles compared to ecosystems like npm, Maven, or Python. License compliance reviews during pull requests are emphasized, as restrictive copyleft licenses can force disclosure of proprietary close-source in-vehicle software, handing blueprints to attackers. Secure distribution involves RBAC, time-based access tokens, and encryption.
- **Stage 2: Aggregation & Risk Prioritization:** Aggregating SBOMs across varied repositories and microservices into an application-level view resolves discrepancies in transitive dependencies. Fraser discusses adapting CISA's Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) into a tailored decision matrix based on application criticality, external exposure, and exploitability. He cautions that remediations should be analyzed holistically, as upgrading packages (e.g., migrating Bootstrap versions) can inadvertently introduce worse CVEs.
- **Stage 3: Supplier Ingestion & Third-Party Governance:** OEMs must enforce strict machine-verifiable SBOM policies on suppliers. Relying on generic PURLs (e.g., type 'generic' or Conan PURLs without an associated OS ecosystem) strips vulnerability mapping capabilities. Automating ingestion allows organizations to ingest supplier VEX statements, codify automated ignore rules for non-exploitable flaws, and pinpoint genuine exposure.

### Takeaways
To achieve mature software supply chain security, automotive organizations should generate SBOMs post-build, prioritize rich component identifiers (PURLs) over generic descriptors, and combine VEX/VDR automation with customized risk evaluation frameworks (like SSVC). Ultimately, buyers are refusing software and hardware from suppliers incapable of delivering accurate, dynamic bills of materials.

talks.title: Implementing Continuous Threat Exposure Management CTEM
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn how CTEM ties breach simulation, lake-scale detection engineering, and codified response playbooks into one cycle.
talks.summary:
Connected vehicle and enterprise growth exposed limits of periodic testing and a traditional SIEM that could not keep pace with telemetry rising from roughly 150 gigabytes to more than ten terabytes per day. The team describes three linked pains: inconsistent defense, a scalability trap that fueled alert fatigue, and manual workflows that stretched mean time to resolution.

Preparation is treated as ongoing engineering rather than a checklist. Threat intelligence, red-team input, and other programs feed scenario design; OpenBASS emulates TTPs to validate detection-as-code and playbooks-as-code as environments change. In-house platforms collect and stream logs (Streams, Vector), land normalized events in a Databricks lake (Trails), correlate observations (Eddie), route alerts (Fire alarms), and orchestrate modular YAML playbooks with peer review for risky actions (Fire Ranger). GenAI augments case context; searches inject observables at runtime and attach large result sets as CSV while preserving executable SQL in case notes.

The closing view maps NIST preparation, detect, respond, and recover into one feedback loop where simulation output drives dashboards and fixes before incidents. The practical takeaway is that a small team can pair open-source BAS with codified detections and response to prove control effectiveness continuously and shrink investigation time.

talks.title: KEYNOTE | Are We There Yet Charting the Course for Long Term Vehicle Security
talks.teaser: Examines how automotive security should be measured and funded across decades of vehicle life.
talks.summary:
The keynote asks where automotive cyber security stands and how it got there. The presenter, from Bosch, traces the field from the CAN bus in 1982 and a hardware security module reference design around 2010 to security requirements becoming standard by 2018. In 2025, the focus has shifted toward compliance, with countries setting conflicting rules that fragment the market.

The central problem is measurement. Vehicles stay in service for decades, attackers are never seen directly, and passing audits or regulations does not prove a product is secure. The presenter contrasts quality management, which checks conformance to fixed specifications, with security, which must hold against adaptive attackers. Pitfalls named include a checklist mindset, a funding model that treats patching as a finite one-time budget, and a rising chance of security findings as the fleet matures. A shared cryptographic key across many units may pass every functional test yet carry serious risk. Layered defenses such as secure hardware, message authentication, domain segmentation, firewalls and intrusion detection are reviewed, with caution about letting detection systems override safety functions. The medieval fortress of Carcassonne serves as an analogy, since its walls failed in a two-week siege.

The closing argues for a trust model that is dynamic, nuanced and adaptive, grading how much a vehicle should trust a message against the action it would trigger instead of a simple yes or no. It also calls for new metrics that leaders can understand and clearer communication up and down the supply chain. Practitioners are advised to prepare data that answers how far along the program really is.

talks.title: Simulating and Evaluating Incident Response for Automotive Systems
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Simulating and Evaluating Incident Response for Automotive Systems.
talks.summary:
### Overview
With connected vehicles increasingly exposed to cyber threats—highlighted by recent events such as the Upstream report noting 409 incidents (92% remote) and the CARIAD/Volkswagen data breach disclosure at the Chaos Communication Congress affecting over 800,000 vehicles—automotive organizations must shift their mindset from *if* an incident occurs to *when*. Presenters Felix Boing and Sergey Va argue that product security must adopt preparedness techniques proven in military war games, IT disaster recovery, and fire drills. Specifically, the automotive sector needs structured ways to simulate and evaluate incident response rather than relying purely on passive documentation or compliance checklists.

### Key Topics
The speakers outline three primary approaches to incident exercises, balancing effort against realism:
1. **Tabletop Exercises**: Low effort, low realism. These are transparent, discussion-based walkthroughs where facilitators guide teams through playbooks, emergency plans, and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). They serve as a low-cost starting point to establish baseline process awareness.
2. **Incident Simulations**: Balanced effort and realism. Considered the "sweet spot" for continuous readiness, these exercises take place within the actual process setting with only selected stakeholders aware. Facilitators introduce realistic stimuli and operational stressors.
3. **Red Teaming**: High effort, high realism. Realistic offensive engagements mirroring external threat actors. While offering authentic testing, red teaming requires extensive reconnaissance, specialized skills across hardware and protocols, significant time (weeks to months), and suffers from limited observability into internal defender workflows.

The exercises involve three core roles:
- **Red Team**: Offensive security executing vulnerability exploitation and compromise.
- **Blue Team**: Defensive personnel mitigating threats and executing incident response.
- **White Team**: Neutral facilitators coordinating the playbook, maintaining rules of engagement, injecting stressors, and documenting observations.

### Technical Details & Playbook Design
Simulations rely on structured playbooks defining triggers, participant boundaries, metrics, and evaluation criteria:
- **Stimulus & Intake Evaluation**: In a technical baseline example, an external researcher submits a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability report alongside a proof of concept. The exercise tracks the incident intake process across the Vehicle Security Operations Center (VSOC) manager, software platform manager, and VSOC analysis team.
- **Containment & Scope Management**: To prevent unnecessary engineering costs, specific stakeholders (such as the platform manager) are pre-notified so developers do not spend resources writing actual fixes for simulated bugs.
- **Metrics**: Key measurements include external reachability (availability of contact points such as `security.txt` or website forms), intake response time, stakeholder notification coverage, and triage accuracy (evaluating whether the RCE's severity is classified correctly).
- **Resilience Tweaks & Stressors**: Scenarios can be adapted to test real-world friction, such as receiving non-technical complaints from an angry customer reporting sensitive infotainment data, key personnel being absent (e.g., manager on vacation), or legacy ECU support where the original engineering team has moved on to newer vehicle architectures.

### Takeaways
- **Move Beyond Passive Compliance**: Standard audits under frameworks like ISO/SAE 21434 often only verify written incident plans or tracking spreadsheets; live simulations prove whether the capabilities actually function in practice.
- **Address the Tier Supplier Blind Spot**: While OEMs are typically at the forefront of public vulnerability disclosures, Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers often lack dedicated incident response readiness for product security despite being reliant on OEM handoffs.
- **Practice Delivers Competence**: Discussion-based tabletops are ideal for initial orientation, but regular incident simulations (recommended at least semi-annually, echoing guidance from Germany's BSI) provide the optimal cost-benefit ratio for training, verifying process efficiency, and removing organizational blind spots.

talks.title: Offensive Security Engineering Why your TARA needs a reality check
talks.teaser: Argues that automotive threat assessments need penetration-test validation to replace guessed attack feasibility ratings.
talks.summary:
The talk examines threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) in automotive cyber security, as framed by ISO 21434. The speaker argues that many assessments rely on theoretical attacker models, and that the attack feasibility ratings they depend on are rarely checked. The attack potential method is walked through in detail, with its five factors: elapsed time, expertise, knowledge, window of opportunity and equipment. The speaker explains that the standard borrows this method from Common Criteria (ISO 15408), and that CVSS and attack vector approaches fit abstract threats poorly.

The main gap is validation. Common Criteria pairs each rating with independent penetration testing, while ISO 21434 testing only covers requirements and cyber security goals, so the attack potential assumptions are never tested. The speaker describes maturity levels where pentesting usually happens once, before start of production or at type approval, with no feedback into the TARA. Testers rarely take on reverse engineering or glitching, and cyber security engineers seldom have pentesting backgrounds.

Recommendations include turning attack steps into test cases that record time, personnel, skill and equipment, so results can raise or lower feasibility ratings. Other points were cross-skilling engineers in penetration testing, creating an offensive engineering role that tracks current attacks, and building in-house capability with automation so external testers can go deeper. In the Q&A, the speaker said in-house people come before tooling, and that side-channel attacks are often left out of assessments. Hands-on practice and capture-the-flag events were suggested for newcomers.

talks.title: Exploit Story Reverse Shells on the Road Hacking Vehicle Infotainment
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Exploit Story Reverse Shells on the Road Hacking Vehicle Infotainment.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at the Secure Our Streets conference as an 'Exploit Story', automotive cybersecurity researcher Abhay Vishnoi (Lead Security Researcher at KPIT India) demonstrates how vehicle infotainment systems can be compromised to establish a persistent reverse shell and potentially interact with the vehicle's CAN bus. The presentation explores hardware and network attack surfaces, privilege escalation techniques, firmware extraction, and the real-world implications of compromising in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) systems.

### Key Topics
- **Infotainment Attack Surfaces**: Examining entry points including USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, UART, open network ports, and over-the-air (OTA) update mechanisms.
- **Access and Privilege Escalation**: Transitioning from locked or restricted shells (via UART or ADB) to full root/superuser access.
- **Firmware Carving and Modification**: Desoldering or tearing down eMMC flash chips, analyzing binaries, extracting boot images and VBmeta partitions, and patching via Magisk.
- **Persistence and Post-Exploitation**: Injecting custom BusyBox binaries, establishing persistent netcat reverse shells via init scripts, defacing boot logos, and exfiltrating personally identifiable information (PII).
- **CAN Bus Interaction and Defense-in-Depth**: Assessing the risks of CAN service manipulation and discussing production mitigations such as hardware protection, network isolation, and secure firmware design.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware & Firmware Extraction**: For systems where UART is locked or ADB is unavailable, the speaker detailed hardware teardown methods. Using tools like TNM programmer on desoldered eMMC chips (demonstrated on a Rockchip-based unit) or software like SP Flash Tool for MediaTek SoCs (specifically MT8163), researchers can extract full flash dumps (`MIMMC.bin`). Using `binwalk` and `dd`, researchers carve out crucial partitions like the kernel, boot image, and `vbmeta` image. To bypass Android Verified Boot (AVB), the boot image is patched (e.g., via Magisk) alongside modified `vbmeta` to disable verification checks before sideloading via Fastboot.
- **Network Exploitation & Live Demo**: In the live demonstration of an aftermarket Android-based infotainment unit, the device's IP (`10.167.88.36`) was scanned using Nmap, revealing open port `5555` (ADB). After connecting directly via ADB, the presenter uploaded an ARMv7-compatible custom BusyBox binary to `/data/local/tmp` (a typically writable directory). A netcat listener was started (`0766`) to establish a reverse shell back to a Kali Linux terminal. Persistence can be achieved by placing the reverse shell command into system init/daemon scripts under `/etc`.
- **CAN Bus and Data Risks**: Post-exploitation reconnaissance revealed running CAN services such as `com.nw.kan`. The speaker noted that while aftermarket units often lack full CAN utilities without custom DBC files, compromising CAN services in production or fleet vehicles (such as a previous test against an electric bus) allows attackers to kill critical services or inject messages. Furthermore, compromised units expose sensitive PII including contacts, emails, microphone feeds, and IP camera streams.

### Takeaways
Aftermarket and connected infotainment systems frequently lack robust default security, often leaving debugging interfaces like ADB or UART accessible. Once a reverse shell is established, attackers can achieve persistence, modify firmware, steal personal user data, and manipulate CAN communication interfaces. Mitigating these risks in production requires rigorous defense-in-depth: hardening hardware against physical debugging/readout, enforcing Android Verified Boot, maintaining strict network isolation between IVI and safety-critical vehicle buses, and applying regular secure OTA patches.

talks.title: Edge AI in Automotive Cybersecurity Challenges and Opportunities
talks.teaser: Shows how AI threat detection on in-vehicle processors can flag attacks locally, reducing cloud upload costs and delays.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why automotive security monitoring is struggling with cloud-only models. The speakers argue that uploading logs from large vehicle fleets is costly, that detection models are slow to retrain, and that false positives and the difficulty of telling an attack from a system malfunction overwhelm security operations teams. Their proposal is to move inference into the vehicle, using neural processing units to correlate events from several ECUs and flag known attack patterns without waiting for cloud analysis.

They then describe how the detection models stay current. Threat intelligence and past incidents are turned into attack paths and techniques, the models are fine-tuned and tested, and they are delivered over the air, with only the affected part of a model updated when needed. Development runs in a cloud-native pipeline that tests models against simulated devices, so teams do not depend on physical bench hardware. Engineers review the outputs, and the models are replayed against simulated attack scenarios before deployment.

The live demo ran on an automotive Linux board, with attack scripts generating CPU, memory, Ethernet and CAN traffic. A locally run language model, tuned on threat intelligence, produced an incident report for each anomaly and matched the pattern to a publicly disclosed compromise of BMW vehicle systems. The results appeared on a back-end dashboard for SOC analysts. The speakers claimed up to 60% lower cloud transfer and processing cost and up to 80% less triage time, and concluded that on-vehicle detection complements the cloud rather than replacing it.

talks.title: Crypto Agility in Automotive Real Time Systems in Context of Post Quantum Cryptography
talks.teaser: Benchmarks NIST post-quantum algorithms on automotive microcontrollers to judge which fit real-time ECU crypto agility.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at crypto agility in automotive real-time systems as quantum computers threaten today's asymmetric cryptography. The speakers argue that software-defined vehicles need cryptography that can be updated over the vehicle's lifetime, and that current microcontrollers lack hardware support for the newly selected post-quantum algorithms, so software implementation is required. They frame the work around the AUTOSAR Classic platform, where the crypto stack is split into a service manager, an interface and drivers.

The team presented an open-source C library that ports the NIST-selected algorithms, two key encapsulation mechanisms and three signature schemes, with a wrapper for AUTOSAR Classic. They benchmarked two microcontroller derivatives, the TC277 and the more capable TC399, running only one core with scratch-pad memory and timing with the performance counter. ML-KEM's runtime was acceptable on both chips, while HQC was too heavy for real-time use. Among the signatures, ML-DSA was judged suitable, FN-DSA had fast verification but slow key generation and signing, and SLH-DSA was unsuitable without hardware accelerators.

Memory results showed that RAM, stack and constants grow with the security level, and the smaller TC277 could not run some of the larger variants at all. The takeaway is that memory, runtime and hardware accelerators, not only the choice of algorithm, decide what fits a given ECU, and that accelerators make crypto agility harder. The Q&A also covered whether signature verification could stay on the host instead of an HSM, and whether these chips offer built-in post-quantum support, which neither does.

talks.title: Under the Hood Tracking API Exploits Before They Hit the Road
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed vehicle APIs get abused at fleet scale and how telematics context can help flag suspicious calls.
talks.summary:
The talk examines application programming interfaces in connected vehicles, including remote commands, over-the-air updates, EV charging and dealer tools. The speakers argue that many recent incidents start in telematics and cloud back ends rather than inside the car, and that attackers favour reusable, scalable entry points. A common pattern begins with collecting vehicle identification numbers from listings and paperwork, then querying lookup endpoints that trust the number as if it were a credential.

Further cases included a VIN-spraying approach, where identifiers are iterated against APIs to bind unauthorised users to cars, and a dealer flow where a license plate could be pivoted into remote vehicle functions. One developer-level example returned owner details and service history with no authorisation or rate limiting. The core problem is a blind spot: gateways check identity and rate limits but not vehicle state, so commands such as unlock or remote start can be approved when pairing history, location or ignition make them implausible.

Their mitigation checklist covered live inventories of endpoints and vehicles, joining API transactions with telematics data, applying common API risk fixes, tuning detections through production feedback and purple-team exercises, standardising checklists and automated tests, and using AI mainly for triage. In the Q&A they stressed that automotive API flaws can have physical safety consequences and that charging and grid links make protection an ecosystem responsibility.

talks.title: Source vs Binary code analysis Challenges and Solutions within the Software Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Explores source versus binary analysis, SBOM practices, and VEX workflows for automotive software supply chain vulnerability management.
talks.summary:
The session situates vulnerability management across the automotive product lifecycle, from design and development through vehicles already in the field. Modern ECUs blend proprietary in-house code, open-source components, third-party libraries, and bought-in modules, while regulations and a fast-moving threat landscape demand continuous monitoring, fleet-wide visibility, and rapid response.

A central thread is transparency via software bills of materials in formats such as CycloneDX and SPDX, built from metadata and source where possible and from firmware binaries when vendors withhold code. The speaker contrasts source composition analysis (including dependency-oriented tooling that relies on an existing SBOM and public CVE data) with binary analysis for post-build images and third-party ECUs. Log4Shell and Heartbleed show how each approach misses issues the other can catch, arguing for combined use. Detection pipelines map listed components to industry identifiers, produce large vulnerability inventories, and then lean on prioritization, vendor coordination, vulnerability disclosure reporting, VEX statements for real-world exploitability, and CSAF-style machine-readable alerts to automate triage.

Closing guidance favors automated SBOM creation, dual analysis to shrink blind spots, standards and APIs across the lifecycle, and structured exchanges with tier suppliers when fixes sit outside the integrator’s control.

talks.title: Automotive Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment Data sharing using openXSAM format
talks.teaser: Presents a survey-based study on converting automotive threat analysis data to the OpenXSAM format for supplier data sharing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how automotive threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) data could be converted into the OpenXSAM format so that cybersecurity information moves more reliably across the vehicle supply chain. The speaker frames the problem around connected vehicles, where standards such as ISO/SAE 21434 and UNECE R155 push manufacturers toward managed security processes, while many teams still depend on proprietary formats and manual handling.

The study combined a 22-question online survey of automotive and cybersecurity professionals with a review of academic papers, industry reports and technical documentation. Respondents came from tier one and tier two suppliers, OEMs, consultancies and universities. Around 70% reported data integrity or compatibility problems when sharing security data. The top challenges were the lack of a universal standard (66.7%) and inconsistent data formats between suppliers (63.3%), and 43.3% said they were not familiar with OpenXSAM. Among the 11 respondents who knew the format, all cited simplified data sharing with suppliers and partners as a benefit, and 90.9% cited better interoperability between systems.

Automating TARA data conversion was rated as likely to improve efficiency, with an average of 4.07 out of five, even though 53.3% of respondents still converted data manually. The speaker recommended building an automation tool that supports multiple input formats and includes automated validation, promoting standard formats through industry collaboration and training, and protecting data confidentiality during conversion. In the question session, the speaker noted that only one tool was known to support OpenXSAM, that version 1.0 cannot yet link TARA results to penetration test evidence, and that exchanged files should be classified and protected like any other customer specification.

talks.title: PIVOT Catalyzing the Community Around Collection and Sharing of Automotive Research Datasets 1
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PIVOT Catalyzing the Community Around Collection and Sharing of Automotive Research Datasets 1.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at the ASRG Secure Our Streets conference, David Balenson (associate director and interim director of the Networking and Cybersecurity Division at USC Information Sciences Institute) introduces the PIVOT project. PIVOT is a collaborative effort involving USC ISI, Colorado State University, the University of Memphis, and industry partner Geotab. Funded under the US National Science Foundation (NSF) Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE) Community Research Infrastructure (CCRI) program, the grant began in October 2022 with plans to run through 2025 or 2026. Rather than conducting primary research itself, PIVOT focuses on developing a community platform to curate, collect, and share automotive and heavy-duty vehicle datasets and tools for vehicle cybersecurity, intelligent transportation, and smart/connected communities.

### Key Topics
The project is structured around five core pillars:
- **Platform:** The core interactive software/hardware infrastructure hosted at the University of Memphis (mirrored at CSU), incorporating a web portal, a catalog based on CooNDA (from the NSF Clavata/SEARCH projects), an Object Store using MinIO, and an authentication/naming shim.
- **Data:** Three distinct sources of data, spanning passenger cars and heavy trucks.
- **Tools:** Software handling multiple layers of the vehicular data pyramid, from physical layer oscilloscope traces and raw CAN/PDU frames to vehicle signals, fleet aggregations, and high-level analytical tools.
- **Services:** Access control, cataloging, Institutional Review Board (IRB) support, and data privacy services.
- **Community:** Outreach via workshops, webinars, academic/industry partnerships, and educational student challenges.

### Technical Details
PIVOT categorizes its datasets into three primary types:
1. **Community Datasets:** Prior research datasets made visible through PIVOT's portal, such as Oak Ridge National Laboratory's ROAD dataset, Korea University HCRL datasets, Bosch's sinAn, and CSU heavy truck datasets.
2. **Geotab Data:** Sourced via the PIVOT Spindle program (a fleet of ~10 researcher vehicles equipped with Geotab GO9 telematics loggers sharing detailed trip, engine fault, fuel, and speed data via MyGeotab) and Geotab's Altitude analytics platform (providing aggregated transportation and stop analytics across over 4 million vehicles, specifically offering datasets for Denver, CO and Shelby County, TN).
3. **Custom CAN Logger 4:** An open-source, low-cost recording unit equipped with GPS, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, CAN, and Automotive Ethernet recording capabilities intended for crowdsourcing vehicular data across diverse models.

Balenson also reviews outcomes from the April 2024 PIVOT Community Workshop, highlighting Mike Westra's keynote on topics beyond CAN (such as Adaptive AUTOSAR, Automotive Ethernet, and EV charging infrastructure). Workshop breakout sessions emphasized challenges in vehicle data time synchronization across heterogeneous buses, edge filtering, and privacy-preserving techniques.

### Takeaways
Automotive network datasets have historically been fragmented, ad hoc, and challenging to acquire due to architectural variations across vehicle makes and privacy concerns. PIVOT addresses these barriers by establishing standardized community infrastructure, engaging students through competitions (CyberAuto, CyberTruck, CyberTractor, and CyberBoat), and offering data anonymization tools. During the Q&A, Balenson addressed privacy handling (such as Geotab geofencing and Privacy-Enhancing Technologies) and encouraged researchers to contribute datasets, adopt PIVOT infrastructure, and collaborate on future proposals.

talks.title: Observing the Clouds Lessons Learned from Cloud Vulnerabilities for HPCs and Software Containers 1
talks.teaser: Explores how container isolation and eBPF filtering could harden software-defined vehicles, covering CAN traffic and SPI bus access.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether containers can make software-defined vehicles safer, drawing on lessons from cloud infrastructure. As car computing moves to central high-performance units running Linux, the speaker argues that the problems seen in data centres are reappearing. He explains that containers are Linux processes isolated by the kernel, so a kernel or runtime flaw can allow an escape, and that weak privilege settings undermine the safeguards around a container.

Using the Jeep attack as a reference, the speaker walks through its path from the cellular connection to the infotainment unit and then to a microcontroller that was reflashed over the SPI bus. He then shows how eBPF programs, loaded into the kernel at runtime, can inspect CAN frames before they reach a container. A toy example drops frames with invalid IDs and checks data values. A second demo uses kernel tracing to block writes to the SPI bus while the program runs, without touching the application.

The talk also covers offensive use of eBPF. The speaker demonstrates a rootkit-style program that rewrote CAN packets on his own car, so the instrument cluster showed an engine speed of 9,000 RPM, and the change disappeared once the program was unloaded. The takeaway is that eBPF gives a flexible, software-defined layer that can be changed after deployment, but it has to sit on top of firmware verification, which must exist deeper in the chain.

talks.title: Automotive Bug Bounty Program and Lessons Learned
talks.teaser: Walks through an automotive Pwn2Own bug bounty, its 49 zero-days, EV charger attack chain and disclosure lessons.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews the first automotive-only Pwn2Own event, held in Tokyo in January, where 17 teams from nine countries submitted 51 entries against 19 targets in four categories. The entries produced 49 unique zero-day vulnerabilities and over a million in prize money. Most findings hit EV chargers, followed by in-vehicle infotainment head units. The speaker explains how the Zero Day Initiative buys reported bugs and works with vendors to get them fixed and disclosed.

The main lessons concern why old bug classes persist. Stack-based buffer overflows were still the most common finding. Protections such as address space layout randomization, non-executable memory and stack canaries were often missing or switched off, and real-time operating systems typically lack them. Leftovers like open debug interfaces, stale certificates and bundled tools made attacks easier. Disclosure was another problem: vendors sometimes denied issues or quietly worked around them, and no multi-vendor process linked OEMs with tier-one suppliers. One EV charger case was walked through step by step. A command injection in a Wi-Fi password field, reached over a Bluetooth packet, gave a shell. The cloud link skipped server certificate verification, which allowed interception and command injection. A remote-support channel led to cloud credentials that reached hundreds of storage buckets.

The speaker argues that bug bounties and red teaming let a company measure product security and test how its product security incident response team handles reports. Findings should feed back into threat modelling. Internal bounties need clear rules of engagement and defined targets.

talks.title: Application of GenAI LLM's for Threat Scenario Generation for TARA Assessments 1
talks.teaser: Explores using generative AI language models to produce context-driven threat scenarios for automotive TARA risk assessments.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how large language models could generate threat scenarios for threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) in automotive cybersecurity. The speaker explains that TARAs built around ISO 21434 often rely on static spreadsheets and the fixed threat list in UNECE R155 Annex 5, which makes it hard to keep pace with new threats or to tailor scenarios to different vehicle systems, such as body control work compared with EV charging.

The research prototype had two parts. A BERT-based sentence-pair model was trained on CAN ID changes and bit sequences from an open-source CAN dataset, covering fuzzing and spoofing attacks, to detect attacks and predict the next logical sequence; it did not analyse payloads. A second stage took user-entered scenarios plus Annex 5 threats, embedded them in a vector database and used retrieval-augmented generation to produce several scenarios. Each generated scenario was then matched by similarity search to a mitigation technique from Annex 5. The model was run offline so that no system data was sent to public services.

The talk closes with cautions. Generic prompts produce poor output, so inputs should combine the asset, the security objective, the compromised property and feasibility and impact ratings. Downloaded models need integrity checks, and models need ongoing updates and human review. Future work includes extending the approach to other threat taxonomies and attack frameworks, and studying prompt tuning and privacy.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Secure Isolation.

talks.title: Enhancing Automotive Cybersecurity Using Machine Learning techniques to Improve ISO SAE 21434
talks.teaser: Shows how machine learning anomaly detection could make ISO/SAE 21434 automotive risk management proactive instead of reactive.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the ISO/SAE 21434 automotive cybersecurity standard is a strong base but handles risk in a largely static, reactive way. Threat and risk assessments are not refreshed when a security operations center raises a serious alert, and the standard says little about log retention, privacy or data quality.

The speaker proposes a five-layer model for proactive, dynamic risk management. Data comes from in-vehicle bus messages, sensors, telematics and driver behaviour, plus cloud-side assessments, incident history and SOC logs. A preprocessing stage cleans, normalises and extracts features. Because vehicle hardware is constrained, a lightweight anomaly detector runs in the vehicle while a heavier cloud model performs deeper and predictive analysis. In a braking-system case study using anonymised data, an Isolation Forest was chosen for its balance of performance and resource use. Validation of the data and anomaly scores suggested the approach flagged more anomalies than the SOC-based method did.

The speaker recommends new work products for each layer, such as a data integration plan, a threat-intelligence enhancement plan, a preprocessing validation procedure and a model lifecycle management plan. OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers were seen as the main beneficiaries, while Tier 2 suppliers would find design changes harder. Open challenges include data quality, computing limits, ML security and privacy, with anonymisation and consent discussed as mitigations. Future work covers automated responses and privacy.

talks.title: CRISKLE An Integrated Product Security Lifecycle Platform for Enhanced Safety & Security Analysis
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CRISKLE An Integrated Product Security Lifecycle Platform for Enhanced Safety & Security Analysis.

talks.title: vSOC Risk Recharging Dynamically Integrating TARA, Threat Intelligence and Live Monitoring 1
talks.teaser: Shows how threat intelligence, live monitoring and risk assessment keep automotive threat models current.
talks.summary:
The speakers introduce automotive risk recharging, a concept that treats threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) as a continuously updated process rather than a one-time exercise. Risks found only in the field flow from the security operations center and threat intelligence back into the TARA, which then reprioritises what engineering should address.

The first case involves an official offline software version used to authenticate an OEM diagnostic tool, found for sale on a dark web marketplace. It could let an attacker create legitimate accounts and change sensitive settings such as a truck's speed limit. Monitoring flagged a tester used from an unusual location and pattern; the team revoked the certificate and restored the original configuration, and the findings added high-risk assets to the TARA.

The second case started with a recently published CVE allowing remote command execution on a charging station controller from one EV manufacturer, with exploits seen in underground channels. After intelligence flagged it, monitoring was tightened and abnormal activity appeared across several stations in one area. Those stations were deactivated, an automated workflow pushed a remote update, and the models were added to the TARA as high-risk assets. The closing message is an operational mindset: monitor assets, rehearse responses, and integrate intelligence, monitoring and risk assessment so each finding improves the next.

talks.title: The Missing Link How we collect and leverage SBOMs
talks.teaser: Shows how Schneider Electric collects SBOMs and uses them to speed up vulnerability impact checks for Log4j and OpenSSL.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how Schneider Electric made software bills of materials (SBOMs) mandatory for product releases from January 2021, after a utility customer asked for them. Most products, mainly firmware and on-premise applications, can be covered by scanning or supplier files, while software-as-a-service products are out of scope. Files were first kept in shared document storage, then loaded into a dedicated SBOM platform that teams can search.

The main case is vulnerability management. For Log4j, teams were asked whether they were affected, but the SBOM platform let staff search for the library directly and pinpoint the products and versions involved. The same search worked for OpenSSL, where one product line could ship several versions. The first customer security disclosure went out within 48 hours. One product changed from not affected to affected after an upstream supplier reported the flaw, showing how gaps in supplier SBOMs matter.

The speaker closes with obstacles. Many suppliers are reluctant to share SBOMs, component naming is inconsistent, especially for proprietary code, and SPDX and CycloneDX both remain in use. Generating SBOMs from build pipelines is only beginning. For practitioners, the takeaway is to request validated, machine-readable SBOMs from suppliers and to keep them updated per release, while exploitability data stays in advisories rather than in the SBOMs.

talks.title: PANEL DISCUSSION Automotive Privacy - Differentiator or Pain in the Neck
talks.teaser: Panel weighs whether car privacy is a market advantage or a compliance burden, using real data-sharing examples.
talks.summary:
A panel of three discussed how privacy fits into modern cars, weighing personalised mobility services against data protection rules such as GDPR and US state laws. The speakers gave examples of car features that already depend on personal data, from phone pairing and saved home addresses to driver monitoring cameras and in-car health sensors. They argued that consent prompts, long privacy policies and vague wording leave drivers unclear about what is collected and who receives it.

The discussion moved to research and disclosure. One speaker described privacy labels that group collected data into categories such as identifiers, geolocation, biometrics, phone data and inferences, and that group sharing with affiliates, data brokers, government, insurers and service providers. A researcher summarised a study of 25 car brands in which all received a negative privacy rating, with most sharing or selling personal data and many giving data to law enforcement on an informal request. Panelists also raised resold vehicles, where the previous owner's data can stay on the car, and noted that some finance companies in the US and Canada already take responsibility for wiping it.

The closing segment argued that privacy can be a competitive differentiator, citing survey results showing buyers now rank data privacy highly, and that existing laws already cover many of these problems and should be enforced rather than replaced. Panelists criticised deceptive consent screens and stressed clear disclosures and deletion processes. Practical takeaways included auditing what a vehicle collects, building data deletion into ownership changes, and treating privacy as a product feature.

talks.title: An Investigation into Retrievable PII Data from a Mercedes Benz NTG6 IVI Module
talks.teaser: Shows how call logs, phone book and navigation data can be pulled from a car infotainment drive without authentication.
talks.summary:
Richard Harding, a digital forensics master's student, examines whether personal data can be recovered from a Mercedes-Benz NTG6 infotainment module bought secondhand. He begins with the UK legal landscape covering data protection and connected vehicle cyber principles, then reviews Mercedes-Benz's privacy policy. He found the text hard to read and vague about storage periods, cross-border transfers and third-party sharing.

To image the drive, the module was powered up first so its memory chip could unlock the storage, then the drive was attached through a write blocker and imaged with FTK Imager. Working through Autopsy, a Visual Studio plugin and a Linux DLT viewer, he located 546 log files and wrote Python carving scripts that searched for start and end markers to pull out contact cards, call logs, navigation and connected device records, saving hashes and offsets for each. On a 16-file test set, the scripts extracted 741 vCard records covering phone book and call log entries, and 197 usable coordinates plotted a driven route.

Mercedes-Benz replied that similar work had been done before and assured him the NTG7 module would not share the same vulnerabilities. Harding stressed that data remains on the vehicle until overwritten, and that current UK rules do not require it to be cleared. He suggested overwriting stored data with false information as the most practical mitigation, and said future work would look at contact images, source code and a connected vehicle app.

talks.title: Driving Efficiency: Validating Your Security Posture With Sector Relevant Intelligence
talks.teaser: Shows how sector threat intelligence can drive simulations that test whether automotive security controls block real threats.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by introducing Filigran, maker of the open-source OpenCTI and OpenBAS platforms, before turning to threats aimed at the automotive sector in the past year. APT32, also called OceanLotus, is described as a group that has favoured automotive targets since 2019, mainly for industrial espionage, and is linked to Vietnam. Ransomware such as LockBit is highlighted because locked factory machines can halt production, even though the software still circulates after law enforcement action. Phishing and business email compromise round out the list, since many partners and less technical staff can be misled.

The middle section covers the threat intelligence lifecycle: planning collection, gathering indicators and vulnerability data, analysing it against frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK, sharing results and collecting feedback. In the demo, an OpenCTI dashboard ranks threat groups, malware and exploited CVEs reported against the transport sector. A GootLoader report from an open feed is then explored through its linked objects, and its attack patterns become a simulation scenario in OpenBAS. The scenario runs through endpoint agents, and outcomes are checked against EDR data.

The closing message is that intelligence should be used looking forward: teams test their own controls before an attacker does, rather than only matching past indicators against logs. Repeating tests shows detection and prevention rates changing after adjustments, giving managers metrics to justify security decisions.

talks.title: Risk assessment along the supply chain From OEM to Tier 1 to Tier 2 - how does it all fit together
talks.teaser: Shows how threat and risk assessments at OEM, Tier 1 and Tier 2 levels can be aligned in automotive projects.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at automotive development, where an OEM passes vehicle functions to Tier 1 suppliers, who may rely on Tier 2 suppliers for semiconductors or software packages. Each level performs its own threat and risk assessment, and the speaker argues these must be checked for consistency and fitted together. The running example is a steering column lock, where a spoofed lock command could cause unexpected locking while driving.

The OEM view starts from vehicle functions and trust boundaries, using a structured attack-type method to derive threat scenarios and damage ratings. The Tier 1 view zooms into the ECU, listing assets such as the motor position and stored command logs, then rates risk per impact category using an attack potential method. Most risks in the example are reduced, which leads to a cyber security goal and a requirement, such as authenticating the lock command with a message authentication code. A software data flow view then helps derive controls like signed code and protected configuration values. Tier 2 suppliers, serving many customers, must work from assumed assessments.

The closing questions covered practical points. Suppliers should check OEM-provided goals and requirements for contradictions and gaps, since the OEM rarely shares its full assessment. A supplier that will not hand over its assessment can offer a walkthrough instead. Tier 2 security manuals help Tier 1 teams use bought components securely, and skipping impact ratings reduces the spread of risk levels and needs careful review.

talks.title: Redefining OEM Supplier Dynamics Powerful TARA Updates for Effective Requirements Specifications
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Redefining OEM Supplier Dynamics Powerful TARA Updates for Effective Requirements Specifications.

talks.title: Shifting Left Vulnerability Management
talks.teaser: Shows how automotive teams can shift vulnerability management earlier using SBOMs, VEX and risk-based prioritization.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why vulnerability management in the automotive industry has to move earlier in development as vehicles become software-defined. The speakers, both from the VW Group, begin with the growth in published CVEs, noting that the NVD could no longer enrich every entry and that the Linux kernel became its own CNA this year, having issued around 1,600 CVEs so far. They argue that the size of the kernel and the transitive dependencies of modern libraries make manual tracking impractical.

They then describe the regulatory baseline under UNECE R155, which asks for a reasonable response time and leaves much open to interpretation. The hard parts are tracing components through a deep supplier chain, deciding who owns a given risk, and testing across every vehicle variant. Their response is to push work to the left: write security requirements into supplier contracts, keep SBOMs and cryptographic BOMs in CycloneDX with VEX data to remove false positives, and use Dependabot and IDE checks so developers see issues early. They also build a custom prioritization function that combines CVSS, EPSS, the KEV catalog, VEX data and internal risk assessments, since only about 5% of published CVEs are exploited.

The closing takeaways are to design systems that can be tested, keep dependency management explicit, update regularly instead of backporting individual patches, and give development teams early feedback through CI/CD automation. The Q&A touched on proprietary vulnerability disclosure, supplier compliance and recording kernel configuration in SBOMs.

talks.title: Tales from a Penetration Testing Team Insights on Recent Zero Day Automotive Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Walks through four zero-day flaws found in production car ECUs across CAN, Ethernet and cellular links, plus mitigation lessons.
talks.summary:
This talk shares four zero-day vulnerabilities that a penetration testing team found in production automotive electronic control units, such as telematics units and body control modules supplied by clients. The aim is to show the types of flaws in vehicle code and configuration so others can plan mitigations.

The first case was a buffer overflow reached over the CAN bus, where an oversized copy overwrote a nearby pointer and gave a write primitive that led to code execution. The second came from fuzzing service discovery and IPC protocols on an in-vehicle Ethernet stack, which crashed the system but gave only partial program counter control. Chaining the IPC flaw with an internal socket path that carries frames up to 8 kilobytes reached a task with safety-critical permissions. The third was weak cryptography in a remote command scheme, with predictable values, derivable keys and a hardcoded master key that allowed impersonation. The fourth was a cellular path where binary SMS messages reached a parser that did not separate them from an authenticated TLS channel, and an unvalidated file could be replaced.

The speaker argued that these flaws stem from faulty protocol and interface implementations and weak security design, not only from new automotive protocols. Suggested steps include early secure design review, fuzzing during validation, hardening such as CFI, MPUs and ASLR, network segregation, and manual code review late in development. Secure boot helps but does not stop runtime memory corruption.

talks.title: TAF as Steel A practical example for applying Targeted Attack Feasibility in an ECU Project
talks.teaser: Shows how a shared feasibility target can handle automotive legacy ECUs where standard controls don't fit.
talks.summary:
Yanni Kovach introduces targeted attack feasibility, a concept from the publicly available ISO specification 8475, as a shared language for automotive customers and suppliers. Rather than prescribing exact controls, it lets a party state the feasibility an attack should be reduced to. He positions it alongside the assurance level approach and says it can carry over feasibility ratings used in ISO 21434. Three use cases are covered: legacy architectures with limited hardware, differences between an OEM's control and a supplier's equivalent, and technologies the customer's requirements do not cover.

The worked example is a hypothetical 2018 engine control module built on a microcontroller with few security capabilities. Four attack paths are assessed: the debug interface, the CAN bus, software update and diagnostics. The customer's requirements include secure boot and a hardware security module, but the speaker judges secure boot and the HSM infeasible on this hardware. The debug interface can be restricted with an ECU-unique key, and a one-time programmable memory can hold the certificates for diagnostics and software update checks. The residual targets become low feasibility for functional coding attacks and very low for firmware tampering through software update and JTAG.

In the Q&A he stresses that the concept is an optional tool rather than a requirement of the standard, and that it is not meant for vulnerability detection. Reducing impact instead of feasibility is possible in his view but remains a matter for customer and supplier discussion. He could not confirm the release status of the specification. The practical takeaway is a common way to record control effectiveness as evidence in a management system.

talks.title: KEYNOTE: Keeping Car Safe in the Real of Hyper-Converged SDVs
talks.teaser: A keynote maps hyper-converged SDV risks and compares isolation, certification, and memory-safety mitigations.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a defense-architecture thought experiment contrasting maximum isolation with systems that must exchange data bidirectionally, then applies that lens to modern cars where infotainment and braking-related functions still need to communicate. It describes today’s zoned vehicle networks—exposed connectivity, gateway-style interface zones, and safety-critical domains—and why inspecting a narrow set of links made cross-zone attacks relatively constrained.

The core argument is that hyper-converged software-defined vehicles collapse multiple zones onto one system on chip, sharing hypervisors, accelerator firmware, and cryptographic blocks. That widens attack surface and enables paths reminiscent of infotainment compromise, virtual-machine escape, and abuse of safety-related privileges, illustrated with published research on connected vehicles and cross-industry hardware IP flaws. The speaker surveys four commercial patterns—hypervisor-centric consolidation, hardware-assisted partitioning, duplicated silicon, and chiplet packages—and weighs flexibility, auditability, and cost, including a walk-through where flawed secure-element descriptor handling could leak braking credentials.

Practitioners are urged to treat upfront integration savings skeptically when validation, partner coordination, and certification lag complexity. Mitigations discussed include stronger network binding, memory-safe firmware for privileged paths, large-scale cooperative assessment, harmonized product assurance, and wider use of memory-safe languages such as Rust in bootloaders, platform firmware, and shared IPs—while OEMs retain responsibility for the full stack picture.

talks.title: Adam Shostack | A Fully Trained Jedi, You Are Not
talks.teaser: Argues engineers need security skills tied to their jobs, not expert-level training, illustrated with connected vehicle development.
talks.summary:
Adam Shostack argues that expecting every developer to become a security expert, a "Jedi," is an unrealistic goal that drives burnout. Most security problems trace back to code, because developers introduce bugs, skip security features, and build controls that are hard to use. Shifting security left only works, he says, when responsibilities, deliverables and required skills are explicitly defined, since engineers resist change imposed without clear expectations.

He uses Bloom's taxonomy to explain why training often jumps to advanced evaluation before people grasp the basics, which leads engineers to misapply tools such as encryption to problems they do not solve. He suggests chunking the knowledge each role needs and asking what can go wrong, a question he says everyone can answer when encouraged. He argues that many flaws are lightweight and cluster at low levels of system and security knowledge, citing bug bounty programs as evidence.

For developers, he proposes a framework built on STRIDE threats, with "elevation of privilege" renamed "expansion of authority," along with an understanding of parsing and predictability and of kill chains. He presents his book on what every engineer should learn as one attempt to make these ideas accessible. He closes by saying that connected and autonomous vehicle engineers are capable, and that clear expectations could mean less rework, fewer escalations and more predictable delivery.

talks.title: PANEL DISCUSSION Maturity of Cybersecurity Management Systems in Automotive Insights from Auditors
talks.teaser: Automotive auditors describe how mature cyber security management systems are, common audit gaps, and what R155 and ISO 21434 require.
talks.summary:
A panel of automotive cyber security auditors and certification specialists examines how mature cyber security management systems (CSMS) are across the car industry. Panelists agree maturity varies widely. Companies that started early, often by extending an existing safety management system, are well prepared, while late starters under pressure from the 2024 UNECE R155 deadline are still gathering evidence. Europe was described as further ahead than parts of Asia and North America.

Recurring gaps include weak control of documents, requirements, configuration and change management, and processes that are written for cyber security alone and do not fit daily development. Vulnerability management was singled out as a common weak spot, and legacy products often break processes designed for new developments. Auditors said most audits end with non-conformities on the first attempt, and only a couple of well-prepared customers passed first time.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that evidence of use in real projects matters more than documents. Auditors expect a traceable path from vulnerability information to a recorded decision and a rollout plan, drawn from several sources. An ISO 21434 certificate helps suppliers show capability but does not replace R155 evidence, and the panel noted that the regulations still lack minimum criteria for validation and penetration testing.

talks.title: Dr. Nils Weissand Enrico Pozzobon | Fault Injection Attacks on Secure Automotive Bootloaders
talks.teaser: Demonstrates electromagnetic fault injection that bypasses signature checks on automotive gateway ECUs and gains code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk covers electromagnetic fault injection against automotive microcontrollers, using Gateway ECUs as targets because they sit at the root of a vehicle network. Physical access threats such as chip tuning, mileage manipulation and vehicle theft motivate the work. Automotive-grade processors tolerate wide temperature and voltage ranges, so the speakers could push them outside their operating range before they failed.

The attack targets the UDS software update flow, in which a bootloader authenticates through security access, erases flash, writes a new image and runs a signature check before starting the application. Security access algorithms are publicly documented and OEM repair tools circulate widely, so an attacker can write a malicious image into the application area, but the signature check blocks it. Coil position, pulse duration, charge voltage and trigger offset were tuned, and a genetic algorithm scored outcomes using stack traces and exception data. On PowerPC, about one success occurred per four million attempts without a search, but over 50 percent after around 10,000 attempts, with the full attack estimated at about half an hour. The same injection position on ARM gave roughly a 5 percent chance.

On PowerPC, a misaligned stack pointer seemed to cause most jumps to payload, and a successful glitch allowed memory dumps, JTAG re-enabling and flash writes. Suggested mitigations include memory protection units that block execution in the bootloader early in boot, running the bootloader from a hardware security module, and redesigning the UDS update process so writable memory is never executable. Findings were reported to the affected OEMs in April 2022.

talks.title: Session 6 | Stage 1 | Peter Maynard | Networks in Flux The Significance of Dynamic Networks within
talks.teaser: Maps 5G network slicing to teleoperated taxi services and shows how zero trust can tighten multi-slice vehicle security.
talks.summary:
The session opens with background on critical infrastructure security research and current work on trust and lightweight authentication for machine-oriented networks. The core technical segment explains 5G network slicing: one physical mobile footprint divided into software-defined slices that offer different latency, throughput, reliability, and isolation for IoT, healthcare, and broadband customers, with slice tenants responsible for their own security.

A teleoperated autonomous taxi scenario illustrates why operators doubt public 5G. Routing, entertainment, council permits, and low-latency command-and-control need different slice qualities, yet all converge on one vehicle, weakening isolation and pushing fleets toward unscalable private roadside networks. Classic 5G security still treats authenticated devices as persistently trusted inside a slice, which breaks down when a single vehicle spans several slices over shared infrastructure.

The close applies zero trust—assume no asset is trusted, grant least privilege for limited periods, and continuously verify integrity—to restrict cross-service abuse (for example, locking in-vehicle broadband to a single streaming destination) and improve confidence for teleoperation. The speaker also asks whether per-vehicle on-demand slices or simpler models might suffice, and notes prior zero-trust deployments in enterprise and in-vehicle environments.
